Day 72 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Pods

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

A Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable compute object and groups one or more tightly coupled containers that share a network context and selected storage.

Architecture / mental model

Pod
├─ app container
├─ optional helper container
├─ shared Pod IP / port space / localhost
└─ explicitly mounted volumes

How it works

Most Pods contain one primary application container, while helper containers can live in the same Pod when they genuinely need the same lifecycle and network context.

Containers in one Pod share the Pod network namespace, including the same Pod IP and port space. They can communicate through localhost rather than discovering one another through cluster networking.

Volumes are shared only when mounted into the containers that need them. A Pod therefore creates a close coupling boundary, not a general-purpose replacement for a multi-service application topology.

Hands-on reference

kubectl run web --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl get pod web -o wide
kubectl describe pod web
kubectl exec web -- hostname -i

Verification

Create a Pod, inspect its assigned node and Pod IP, then run a command inside it. For a multi-container lab, verify localhost communication and explicitly shared volumes.

Field note / gotcha

A Pod is not Docker Compose wearing a Kubernetes badge. Separate application services normally deserve separate controllers/Pods so they can scale and fail independently.

Security considerations

Pod-level privilege settings, service-account tokens, host mounts and shared namespaces determine how much a compromised container can reach. Co-location increases trust between containers in the same Pod.

What I learned

The Pod is the scheduling and lifecycle unit, so container grouping should reflect genuine lifecycle coupling.
